<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:closed-subdcpo}
Let $D$ be a dcpo and let $C\in\Gamma(D)$ be nonempty. Then
\[
  \Gamma(C)=\{F\in\Gamma(D):F\subseteq C\}
            =\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\Gamma(D)}C.
\]
Moreover,
\[
  \operatorname{Irr}(\Gamma(C))=\{A\in\operatorname{Irr}(\Gamma(D)):A\subseteq C\}
          =\operatorname{Irr}(\Gamma(D))\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\Gamma(D)}C.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
A subset $F\subseteq C$ is lower in $C$ if and only if it is lower in $D$,
because $C$ is lower. Directed subsets of $F$ have the same suprema in $C$
and $D$. This proves the first equality. The second follows because
irreducibility is tested against finite unions of Scott-closed sets, whose
restrictions to $C$ are precisely the Scott-closed sets of $C$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:principal-directed-join}
Let $A$ be a directed subset of a dcpo $D$. Then
\[
  \bigvee_{\Gamma(D)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Da:a\in A\}=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_D\bigvee A.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The right-hand side is a Scott-closed upper bound of the family. Conversely,
any Scott-closed set containing every $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Da$ contains $A$, hence contains
$\bigvee A$ and therefore $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_D\bigvee A$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:Skula-density-equivalence}
Let $D$ be a dcpo and let $P\subseteq D$ be any subset. Then $P$ is Skula-dense in $\Sigma D$ if and only if
\[
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx
  \qquad(x\in D).
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
A basic Skula neighbourhood of $x$ is $O\cap C$, where $O$ is Scott open and $C$ is Scott closed, with $x\in O\cap C$. Since $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx\subseteq C$, every such neighbourhood contains $O\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$. Conversely, $O\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$ is itself Skula open. Thus $P$ is Skula-dense exactly when every Scott-open neighbourhood $O$ of every $x$ meets $P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$, that is, when $x\in\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)$. This closure is contained in $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$ and is lower, so the latter condition is equivalent to the displayed equality.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:E2}
A morphism $e:A\to B$ belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$ if $e^*$ is an isomorphism of
dcpos. Such a morphism is called \emph{$2$-equable}. Equivalently,
\(
  e^{-1}:\sigma(B)\longrightarrow\sigma(A)
\)
is an order isomorphism. The full subcategory
$\mathcal R_2=E_{\mathbf 2}^{\perp}$ is the reflective hull of $\mathbf 2$ in $\mathbf{DCPO}$ \cite[Theorem~2.7]{HeLyuChenKou2026}. We write
\(
  \lambda_D:D\longrightarrow L_2 D
\)
for the $\mathcal R_2$-reflection unit.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:reflection-package}
For every dcpo $D$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item The reflection unit $\lambda_D$ belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$ and induces order
      isomorphisms
      \[
        \sigma(L_2 D)\cong\sigma(D),\qquad
        \Gamma(L_2 D)\cong\Gamma(D).
      \]
\item If $D\in\mathcal R_2$ and $e:D\to E$ belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$, then $e$ is an
      isomorphism in $\mathbf{DCPO}$.
\item The category $\mathcal R_2$ is $\Gamma$-faithful.
\item Every $C_{\sigma}$-unique dcpo belongs to $\mathcal R_2$.
\item Every sober dcpo belongs to $\mathcal R_2$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:E2-image}
The class $E_{\mathbf 2}$ contains all isomorphisms and is closed under composition.
If $e:A\to B$ belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$, then $e$ is an order embedding, its image
$e[A]$ is a sub-dcpo of $B$, and the inclusion $j:e[A]\hookrightarrow B$
belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The first two assertions follow from
$(g\circ e)^{-1}=e^{-1}\circ g^{-1}$ on Scott-open sets. By
\cite[Lemma~3.4]{HeLyuChenKou2026}, surjectivity of
$e^{-1}:\sigma(B)\to\sigma(A)$ implies that $e$ is an order embedding and
that $e[A]$ is a sub-dcpo of $B$. Let $\bar e:A\to e[A]$ be the
corestriction. It is a dcpo isomorphism and $e=j\circ\bar e$. On open sets,
$e^{-1}=\bar e^{-1}\circ j^{-1}$. Both $e^{-1}$ and $\bar e^{-1}$ are
order isomorphisms, hence so is $j^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:E2-subdcpo}
A sub-dcpo $P\subseteq D$ is \emph{$2$-equable} if its inclusion belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$. Equivalently, restriction is an order isomorphism
\[
  \rho:\Gamma(D)\longrightarrow\Gamma(P),\qquad C\longmapsto C\cap P.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:closure-characterization}
Let $P\subseteq D$ be a sub-dcpo. Then $P$ is $2$-equable if and only if
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)&=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx
     &&\text{for every }x\in D, \tag{SD}\label{eq:SD}\\
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(A)\cap P&=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(P)}(A)
     &&\text{for every }A\subseteq P. \tag{SC}\label{eq:SC}
\end{align}
When these conditions hold, restriction has inverse $C\mapsto\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(C)$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Write $\rho(C)=C\cap P$ and first suppose that $\rho$ is an order isomorphism. For $x\in D$, set $H=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)$. Then $H\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$ and $H\cap P=(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)\cap P$. Injectivity gives $H=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$, proving \eqref{eq:SD}.

For $A\subseteq P$, continuity of the inclusion gives
\[
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(P)}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(A)\cap P.
\]
Choose $G\in\Gamma(D)$ with $G\cap P=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(P)}(A)$. Since $A\subseteq G$, one has $\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(A)\subseteq G$, which proves the reverse inclusion and hence \eqref{eq:SC}.

Conversely, assume \eqref{eq:SD} and \eqref{eq:SC}. If $G,H\in\Gamma(D)$ have the same trace on $P$ and $x\in G$, then $P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx\subseteq H$. By \eqref{eq:SD}, $x\in H$. Interchanging $G$ and $H$ proves injectivity of $\rho$. If $C\in\Gamma(P)$, then \eqref{eq:SC} gives $\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(C)\cap P=C$. Thus $\rho$ is bijective with the stated monotone inverse, and hence is an order isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:directed-lifting-bridge-density}
Let $P\subseteq D$ be a sub-dcpo. It has \emph{directed lifting} if, whenever $E\subseteq D$ is directed and $p\in P$ satisfies $p\leq\bigvee E$, there is a directed set $B\subseteq P$ with $\bigvee B=p$ such that each $b\in B$ lies below some member of $E$.
It has \emph{bridge density} if, for each $x\in D$, there is a directed set $V_x\subseteq D$ with $\bigvee V_x=x$ such that every $v\in V_x$ admits $p_v\in P$ with $v\leq p_v\leq x$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:directed-lifting-bridge-density}
Bridge density implies \eqref{eq:SD}, and directed lifting implies \eqref{eq:SC}. Hence the two conditions together make $P\hookrightarrow D$ $2$-equable.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Under bridge density, every $v\in V_x$ lies below a point of $P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$. Consequently, its Scott closure contains $V_x$, then $x=\bigvee V_x$, and hence all of $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$. This proves \eqref{eq:SD}.

Assume directed lifting. For $C\in\Gamma(P)$ put
\[
  H_C=\{x\in D:P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx\subseteq C\}.
\]
This is a lower set. Let $E\subseteq H_C$ be directed and let $p\in P$ satisfy $p\leq\bigvee E$. Choose a lifting set $B\subseteq P$ with supremum $p$. For every $b\in B$, some $e\in E$ satisfies $b\leq e$; since $e\in H_C$, one has $b\in C$. Thus $B\subseteq C$, and Scott closedness of $C$ gives $p\in C$. Therefore $\bigvee E\in H_C$, so $H_C\in\Gamma(D)$.

Since $C$ is lower in $P$, one has $H_C\cap P=C$. For $A\subseteq P$, take $C=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(P)}(A)$. The inclusion $A\subseteq H_C$ gives
\[
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(D)}(A)\cap P\subseteq H_C\cap P=C.
\]
The reverse inclusion follows from continuity of $P\hookrightarrow D$. This proves \eqref{eq:SC}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The two implications above are only sufficient conditions and are not reversible in general. For instance, the initial sub-dcpo \(P^\times_0\subseteq K\times\mathbb I\) constructed in Section~\ref{sec:product-counterexample} satisfies \textup{(SD)} but not bridge density. On the other hand, if
\(
D=\{\bot,p,\top\}\cup\{e_n:n\in\mathbb N\},
\)
with \(\bot<e_0<e_1<\cdots<\top\) and \(\bot<p<\top\), where \(p\) is incomparable with every \(e_n\), then taking \(P=D\) gives \textup{(SC)} while directed lifting fails.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:canonical-envelope}
For dcpos $D$ and $Q$, one has $\Gamma(Q)\cong\Gamma(D)$ if and only if $Q$ is isomorphic to a $2$-equable sub-dcpo of $L_2D$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If $\Gamma(Q)\cong\Gamma(D)$, then
\[
  \Gamma(L_2Q)\cong\Gamma(Q)\cong\Gamma(D)\cong\Gamma(L_2D).
\]
By $\Gamma$-faithfulness of $\mathcal R_2$, there is an isomorphism $h:L_2Q\to L_2D$. The composite $h\circ\lambda_Q$ belongs to $E_{\mathbf 2}$. Its image is the required sub-dcpo by \cref{lem:E2-image}.

Conversely, if $Q$ is isomorphic to a $2$-equable sub-dcpo $P\subseteq L_2D$, then $\Gamma(Q)\cong\Gamma(P)\cong\Gamma(L_2D)\cong\Gamma(D)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:intrinsic-rigidity}
For a dcpo $D$, the following are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $D$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
\item The dcpo $L_2D$ has no proper $2$-equable sub-dcpo.
\item $D\in\mathcal R_2$, and every sub-dcpo $P\subseteq D$ satisfying \eqref{eq:SD} and \eqref{eq:SC} equals $D$.
\end{enumerate}
Equivalently, the sub-dcpos in \textup{(ii)} may be specified by \eqref{eq:SD} and \eqref{eq:SC} in the ambient dcpo $L_2D$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that $D$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique. Then $D\in\mathcal R_2$ by \cref{thm:reflection-package}(iv). If $P\subseteq L_2D$ is $2$-equable, then $\Gamma(P)\cong\Gamma(D)$, so $P\cong D$ and $P\in\mathcal R_2$. By \cref{thm:reflection-package}(ii), the inclusion $P\hookrightarrow L_2D$ is itself an isomorphism, hence is surjective. Thus $P=L_2D$.

Assume \textup{(ii)}. By \cref{lem:E2-image}, the image of $\lambda_D$ is a $2$-equable sub-dcpo of $L_2D$. It must be all of $L_2D$, so $\lambda_D$ is an isomorphism and $D\in\mathcal R_2$. Identifying $D$ with $L_2D$ and applying \cref{thm:closure-characterization} proves \textup{(iii)}.

Finally, suppose \textup{(iii)} and $\Gamma(Q)\cong\Gamma(D)$. By \cref{thm:canonical-envelope}, $Q$ is isomorphic to a $2$-equable sub-dcpo $P\subseteq D$. The closure criterion and \textup{(iii)} give $P=D$, and hence $Q\cong D$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:sober-equable-completions}
Let $D$ be sober and let $i:P\hookrightarrow D$ be a $2$-equable sub-dcpo. Then $i$ is both the sobrification map of $\Sigma P$ and the $\mathcal R_2$-reflection of $P$. More precisely,
\[
  \Psi:D\longrightarrow\widehat P,\qquad
  \Psi(x)=P\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx,
\]
is an order isomorphism and a homeomorphism from $\Sigma D$ to the topological sobrification of $\Sigma P$. Consequently,
\[
  D\cong L_2P\cong\widehat P.
\]
If $P\subsetneq D$, then $P\notin\mathcal R_2$ and $\Sigma P$ is not sober.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Restriction $\rho:\Gamma(D)\to\Gamma(P)$ preserves irreducible elements. Since $D$ is sober, all members of $\operatorname{Irr}(\Gamma(D))$ are principal ideals. Hence $\Psi$ is an order isomorphism onto $\widehat P$.

For $C\in\Gamma(P)$, put $G=\rho^{-1}(C)$. Then
\[
  \Psi(x)\subseteq C
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \rho(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)\subseteq\rho(G)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in G.
\]
Thus $\Psi^{-1}(\widehat C)=G$, and $G$ ranges over all of $\Gamma(D)$. This proves that $\Psi$ is a homeomorphism. For $p\in P$, one has $\Psi(i(p))=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Pp$, so $i$ corresponds to the canonical sobrification map.

Moreover, $D\in\mathcal R_2=E_{\mathbf 2}^{\perp}$. Since $i\in E_{\mathbf 2}$, precomposition induces $[D\to R]\cong[P\to R]$ for every $R\in\mathcal R_2$. This is the universal property of the $\mathcal R_2$-reflection, so $D\cong L_2P$. If $P\in\mathcal R_2$, \cref{thm:reflection-package}(ii) would make $i$ an isomorphism. Hence a proper such $P$ lies outside $\mathcal R_2$ and, in particular, is not sober.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:dominated-facts}
Let $D$ be a dcpo.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item $\widehat D$ is strongly complete.
\item Every principal ideal $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$, regarded as an element of
      $\widehat D$, is $\prec$-compact.
\item If $D$ is dominated, then the $\prec$-compact elements of
      $\widehat D$ are exactly the principal ideals $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$, $x\in D$.
\item Every strongly complete dcpo is dominated. In particular, every sober
      dcpo is dominated.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:directed-generation}
Let $D$ be a dcpo.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item An element $b\in D$ is a \emph{$C_{\sigma}$-unique element} if
      the dcpo $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
\item The dcpo $D$ is \emph{directedly $C_{\sigma}$-generated} if, for every
      $x\in D$, there exists a directed set $B_x\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$
      consisting of $C_{\sigma}$-unique elements such that
      $x=\bigvee B_x$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:local-reconstruction}
Let $D$ be a locally dominated and directedly $C_{\sigma}$-generated dcpo.
Then $D$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $Q$ be a dcpo and let
\(\Phi:\Gamma(D)\longrightarrow\Gamma(Q)\)
be an order isomorphism. If $D=\varnothing$, then $\Gamma(D)$ has one element, so $Q=\varnothing$ and the result is immediate. Assume $D\neq\varnothing$. We construct an order isomorphism $f:D\to Q$ in
three steps.

\emph{Step 1: reconstruction from principal ideals.}
Let $b$ be a $C_{\sigma}$-unique element of $D$. By
\cref{lem:closed-subdcpo}, the restriction of $\Phi$ yields
\[
  \Gamma(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)
  \cong\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\Gamma(D)}(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)
  \cong\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\Gamma(Q)}\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)
  \cong\Gamma\bigl(\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)\bigr).
\]
The Scott-closed set $\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)$ is nonempty and hence is a dcpo with
the inherited order. Since $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique,
$\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)$ has a largest element, denoted by $f(b)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:image-generator}
  \Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db)=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(b).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for $C_{\sigma}$-unique elements $b,c$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generator-order}
  b\leq c\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(b)\leq f(c).
\end{equation}

For $x\in D$, choose a directed set $B_x$ of $C_{\sigma}$-unique elements
with $x=\bigvee B_x$. By \eqref{eq:generator-order}, $f(B_x)$ is directed,
and \cref{lem:principal-directed-join} gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)
  &=\Phi\left(\bigvee_{\Gamma(D)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Db:b\in B_x\}\right)\\
  &=\bigvee_{\Gamma(Q)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(b):b\in B_x\}\\
  &=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Q\left(\bigvee_{b\in B_x}f(b)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)$ has a unique largest element. Define $f(x)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:image-principal}
  \Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x).
\end{equation}
This definition is independent of the choice of $B_x$, and it yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:order-embedding}
  x\leq x'\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\leq f(x').
\end{equation}
Hence $f$ is an order embedding.

\emph{Step 2: preservation of directed suprema.}
If $A\subseteq D$ is directed, then
\cref{lem:principal-directed-join} and \eqref{eq:image-principal} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf\!\left(\bigvee A\right)
  &=\Phi\left(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_D\bigvee A\right)\\
  &=\Phi\left(\bigvee_{\Gamma(D)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Da:a\in A\}\right)\\
  &=\bigvee_{\Gamma(Q)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(a):a\in A\}\\
  &=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Q\bigvee f(A).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:preserves-directed-sups}
  f\!\left(\bigvee A\right)=\bigvee f(A).
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: local domination forces the image to be lower.}
Let $y\leq f(x)$ and put $C=\Phi^{-1}(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qy)$, then $C\in\operatorname{Irr}(\Gamma(D))$. Moreover, $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qy\subseteq\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)$, so
$C\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$. By \cref{lem:closed-subdcpo}, $\Phi$ therefore
restricts to an order isomorphism
\[
  \Gamma(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx)\longrightarrow\Gamma(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x))
\]
and hence to an order isomorphism
\[
  \widehat{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx}\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x)}
\]
that sends $C$ to $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qy$. The relation $\prec$ is invariant under order
isomorphisms of strongly complete dcpos, since such isomorphisms preserve
Scott-closed irreducible subsets and their suprema. By
\cref{prop:dominated-facts}(i),(ii), $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qy$ is $\prec$-compact in
$\widehat{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x)}$, and hence $C$ is $\prec$-compact in
$\widehat{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx}$. Since $D$ is locally dominated, $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx$ is
dominated. Thus \cref{prop:dominated-facts}(iii) gives some $x'\leq x$ with
$C=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx'$. Equation~\eqref{eq:image-principal} now yields
$\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qy=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x')$, and hence $y=f(x')$. Therefore $f(D)$ is lower in
$Q$.

By \eqref{eq:preserves-directed-sups}, $f(D)$ is also closed under directed
suprema in $Q$, and hence is Scott closed. Finally,
\[
  Q=\Phi(D)
   =\bigvee_{\Gamma(Q)}\{\Phi(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx):x\in D\}
   =\bigvee_{\Gamma(Q)}\{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x):x\in D\}.
\]
The Scott-closed set $f(D)$ contains every $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Qf(x)$, so it contains
their join. Hence $f(D)=Q$, and $f$ is an order isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:comparison-xuzhao}
The construction of $f$ from principal ideals and the directed-generation
argument are inherited from \cite[Theorem~3.9]{ZhaoXu2018} and
\cite[Proposition~3.2]{XuZhao2019}. The new step is the proof that $f(D)$ is
lower: local domination principalizes $C$ inside
$\widehat{\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx}$ and thereby replaces the use of bounded sobriety.
Since every bounded sober dcpo is locally dominated, the 2019 result is a
special case. Local domination is strictly weaker in general
\cite[Remark~3.8(2) and Proposition~4.10]{XuZhao2019}, although no strict
separation is claimed within the smaller class of directedly
$C_{\sigma}$-generated dcpos.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:product-strongly-complete}
An arbitrary product of strongly complete dcpos is strongly complete.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $(S_i)_{i\in I}$ be strongly complete dcpos and put
$S=\prod_{i\in I}S_i$. Let $A\subseteq S$ be a nonempty irreducible subset.
Each coordinate projection $\pi_i:S\to S_i$ is Scott continuous, so
$\pi_i(A)$ is nonempty and irreducible. Put $s_i=\bigvee\pi_i(A)$. Then
$s=(s_i)_{i\in I}$ is an upper bound of $A$, and every upper bound $u$ of
$A$ satisfies $s_i\leq u_i$ for all $i$. Hence $s=\bigvee A$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:arbitrary-product}
Let $(D_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of locally quasicontinuous dcpos such that
every point of each $D_i$ lies above a minimal element. Then
$\prod_{i\in I}D_i$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The empty product is a one-element dcpo and is $C_{\sigma}$-unique. If a factor is empty, so is the product, and the conclusion is again immediate. Otherwise put $D=\prod_{i\in I}D_i$ and fix $x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\in D$. Its principal
ideal is order-isomorphic to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:principal-product}
  \mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx\cong\prod_{i\in I}\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{D_i}x_i.
\end{equation}
Each factor on the right is quasicontinuous, hence sober and strongly
complete. By \cref{prop:product-strongly-complete}, the product in
\eqref{eq:principal-product} is strongly complete and therefore dominated
by \cref{prop:dominated-facts}(iv). Thus $D$ is locally dominated.

For each $i\in I$, choose a minimal element $r_i\leq x_i$. For a finite
subset $H\subseteq I$, define $x^H\in D$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-coordinate-truncation}
  x^H_i=
  \begin{cases}
    x_i,&i\in H,\\
    r_i,&i\notin H.
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The family $\{x^H:H\subseteq I\text{ finite}\}$ is directed and has
supremum $x$. Since $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{D_i}r_i=\{r_i\}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:truncation-principal}
  \mathord{{\downarrow}}_Dx^H\cong\prod_{i\in H}\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{D_i}x_i.
\end{equation}
The finite product in \eqref{eq:truncation-principal} is quasicontinuous
\cite[Remark~3.11(i)]{XuZhao2019} and hence $C_{\sigma}$-unique
\cite[Lemma~3.8]{ZhaoXu2018}. Therefore every $x^H$ is a
$C_{\sigma}$-unique element, and $D$ is directedly
$C_{\sigma}$-generated. Apply \cref{thm:local-reconstruction}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:J-arbitrary-power}
For every set $I$, the dcpo $\mathbb J^I$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Apply \cref{thm:arbitrary-product} to the constant family $D_i=\mathbb J$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:product-factor-order}
The dcpo $K$ is countable and has greatest element $\top_K$. Every nonempty
subset $A\subseteq K$ has the coordinatewise supremum
\begin{equation}\label{eq:K-sup}
  \left(\bigvee_K A\right)(i)=\bigvee\{f(i):f\in A\}.
\end{equation}
Finite nonempty infima are also coordinatewise. Moreover, for every
$f\in K$, the principal filter $\mathord{\uparrow}_K f$ contains no infinite antichain.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
There are only countably many finite supports and, on each fixed finite
support, only countably many assignments of positive integers. Thus $K$ is
countable. Choose $f_0\in A$ and let $a$ be the coordinatewise supremum in
\eqref{eq:K-sup}. Since $a\geq f_0$, one has
$\operatorname{supp}(a)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(f_0)$, so $a\in K$; it is plainly the least upper
bound. The assertion about finite infima is immediate from finite support.

For fixed $f\in K$, restriction to $\operatorname{supp}(f)$ gives
\[
  \mathord{\uparrow}_K f\cong
  \prod_{i\in\operatorname{supp}(f)}[f(i),\infty]_{\overline{\mathbb N_{>0}}}.
\]
Every infinite sequence in a well-ordered chain has a nondecreasing
subsequence. Successively passing to subsequences in the finitely many
coordinates gives a coordinatewise nondecreasing subsequence. Hence the
finite product, and therefore $\mathord{\uparrow}_K f$, has no infinite antichain.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:down-directed-closed-K}
If $S\subseteq K$ is closed under nonempty directed suprema computed in
$K$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:down-S-closed}
  \mathord{{\downarrow}}_K S\in\Gamma(K).
\end{equation}
The assertion also holds for $S=\varnothing$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The empty case is trivial. Let $B\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_KS$ be directed and choose
$b_0\in B$. The set $B_0=B\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_Kb_0$ is directed and cofinal in $B$. For every $b\in B_0$, choose $s\in S$ with $b\leq s$; then $s\in T=S\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_Kb_0$. Thus $T\neq\varnothing$ and $B_0\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_KT$. Every element of $T$ lies below a maximal element
of $T$: apply Zorn's lemma to $T\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_Ks$, using closure of $S$ under
nonempty directed suprema. By \cref{prop:product-factor-order}, the set of
maximal elements of $T$ is a finite antichain, say
$m_1,\ldots,m_k$. Hence
\(B_0\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^k\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Km_j\).
The right-hand side is a finite union of Scott-closed sets. Therefore
$\bigvee B=\bigvee B_0$ belongs to it and hence to $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_KS$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:K-sober}
The Scott space $\Sigma K$ is sober.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $C\in\Gamma(K)$ be nonempty and irreducible. Since $C$ is Scott
closed, it is a sub-dcpo of $K$. For each $c\in C$, every chain in
$C\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_Kc$ is directed and has its supremum again in $C\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_Kc$.
Zorn's lemma therefore gives a maximal element of $C$ above $c$, and hence
$C=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_K\operatorname{Max}(C)$. Every subset of
$\operatorname{Max}(C)$ has only singleton nonempty directed subsets and is
therefore closed under ambient directed suprema. By
\cref{lem:down-directed-closed-K}, the lower closure of every such subset is
Scott closed in $K$.

If $\operatorname{Max}(C)$ contained two distinct elements, choose
$m\in\operatorname{Max}(C)$. Then
\[
  C=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Km\cup
    \mathord{{\downarrow}}_K\bigl(\operatorname{Max}(C)\setminus\{m\}\bigr)
\]
would express $C$ as the union of two proper Scott-closed subsets,
contradicting irreducibility. Thus $C=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Km$ for a unique $m\in K$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:K-unique}
The dcpo $K$ is $C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Since $K$ is sober, it belongs to $\mathcal R_2$.
By \cref{thm:intrinsic-rigidity}, it suffices to show that
$K$ has no proper $2$-equable sub-dcpo.
Let $S\subseteq K$ be a sub-dcpo for which
restriction $\Gamma(K)\to\Gamma(S)$ is an order isomorphism. Fix $x\in K$.
The set $S_x=S\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Kx$ is closed under ambient directed suprema, so
\cref{lem:down-directed-closed-K} gives
$F_x=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_KS_x\in\Gamma(K)$. Moreover,
\(F_x\cap S=S\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Kx=(\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Kx)\cap S\).
Injectivity of restriction yields $F_x=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Kx$. Since $x\in F_x$, there is
$s\in S_x$ with $x\leq s\leq x$, hence $x=s\in S$. Thus $S=K$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:product-rows}
For every $\tau=(a,H,q)\in\mathcal T_{\times}$, the sequence
$(\operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n))_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$ is strictly increasing and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:row-product-sup}
  \bigvee_{n\in\mathbb N_{>0}}\operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n)=q.
\end{equation}
At the private coordinate $k=h_{\times}(\tau)$ one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:row-private-coordinate}
  \operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n)_K(k)=n.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Write $q=(b,r)$ and $k=h_{\times}(\tau)$. By \eqref{eq:h-product}, both $b(k)$ and
$u^{\times}_{a,H,n}(k)$ equal $\infty$, so \eqref{eq:row-private-coordinate} holds.
The first coordinate of every row has finite support contained in
$\operatorname{supp}(b)\cup H\cup\{k\}$, and the second coordinate belongs to
$\mathbb Q\cap(0,r)$. All coordinates are nondecreasing in $n$, while the
second coordinate is strictly increasing.

On $H$, the first coordinate is $\min\{b(i),n\}$ because $b\leq a$; outside
$H\cup\{k\}$ it is $b(i)$; and at $k$ it increases to
$\infty=b(k)$. The second coordinate increases to $r$. Thus the supremum is
$q$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:product-P-basic}
The set $P_{\times}$ is countable. Every $p\in P_{\times}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:P-product-basic}
  0<p_{\mathbb I}<1,\qquad p_{\mathbb I}\in\mathbb Q,
  \qquad \operatorname{supp}(p_K)\neq\varnothing.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:P-product-no-top-profile}
  P_{\times}\cap(\{\top_K\}\times\mathbb I)=\varnothing.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $P_{\times}$ has no greatest element.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Countability follows from countability of $P^{\times}_{0}$, $\mathcal T_{\times}$ and $\mathbb N_{>0}$.
The marker points satisfy \eqref{eq:P-product-basic}; every new row has
rational height in $(0,1)$ and nonempty support by
\eqref{eq:row-private-coordinate}. Induction gives
\eqref{eq:P-product-basic} and \eqref{eq:P-product-no-top-profile}.

It remains to show that $P_{\times}$ has no greatest element. Fix
$p\in P_{\times}$. By \eqref{eq:P-product-basic}, the finite set
$\operatorname{supp}(p_K)$ is nonempty. Choose
$r\in\mathbb N_{>0}\setminus\operatorname{supp}(p_K)$ and put
\(q=(z^{\times}_{r,1},\beta_r(1))\).
Then $q\in P^{\times}_{0}\subseteq P_{\times}$. Choose any
$s\in\operatorname{supp}(p_K)$. Since $r\notin\operatorname{supp}(p_K)$, we have $s\neq r$, and hence
\(q_K(s)=\infty>p_K(s)\).
Thus $q\nleq p$. Since every $p\in P_{\times}$ fails to dominate some
$q\in P_{\times}$, the poset $P_{\times}$ has no greatest element.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:product-P-dcpo}
 $P_{\times}$ is a sub-dcpo of $X$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Give each $p\inP_{\times}$ a fixed certificate, using its least construction stage
\[
  \operatorname{rk}_{\times}(p)=\min\{m:p\inP^{\times}_{m}\}.
\]
For rank zero, choose a marker representation $p=(f,\beta_i(n))$ with $f(i)=n$ and use $(0,i)$. Otherwise choose $p=\operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n)$ from its first stage, write $\tau=(a,H,q_\tau)$, and use $(1,h_{\times}(\tau))$. The endpoint $q_\tau$ belongs to the preceding stage. In both cases the certificate coordinate belongs to $\operatorname{supp}(p_K)$. For a row certificate, injectivity of $h_{\times}$ determines $\tau$, and the value at that coordinate determines $n$. A private coordinate may occur in other supports; only its use as a row certificate must identify a unique row family.

Let $p_0\leq p_1\leq\cdots$ be increasing in $P_{\times}$ and let $p$ be
its supremum in $X$. Since supports decrease along increasing sequences,
\[
  \operatorname{supp}((p_j)_K)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}((p_0)_K)
  \qquad(j\in\mathbb N).
\]
Only finitely many certificate types and coordinates can therefore occur.
Choose an infinite subsequence with one fixed certificate. Its index set is
unbounded, so the subsequence is cofinal.

In the marker case, the subsequence has the form
$(f_j,\beta_i(n_j))$ with $f_j(i)=n_j$. Monotonicity of the first
coordinates makes $(n_j)$ nondecreasing, while monotonicity of the second
coordinates and strict decrease of $\beta_i$ force $(n_j)$ to be constant,
say $n_j=n$. The cofinal subsequence therefore has constant second
coordinate $\beta_i(n)$ and constant $i$th first coordinate $n$. Its ambient
supremum has the same two coordinates and hence is again a marker in $P^{\times}_{0}$.

In the row case, injectivity of $h_{\times}$ forces all points in the cofinal
subsequence to come from one triple $\tau$, so they are
$\operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n_j)$. The private coordinate makes $(n_j)$ nondecreasing. If it
is bounded, it is eventually constant and the supremum is a retained row.
If it is unbounded, \cref{lem:product-rows} gives supremum $q_\tau$, which
belongs to an earlier construction stage. Hence every increasing sequence
in $P_{\times}$ has its ambient supremum in $P_{\times}$.

Finally, $P_{\times}$ is countable, so every directed subset has an
increasing cofinal sequence. Its ambient supremum therefore belongs to
$P_{\times}$ and is also its supremum in $P_{\times}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:product-Skula-density}
For every $x\in X$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product-TG}
  \operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X)}(P^{\times}_{0}\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Xx)=\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Xx.
\end{equation}
In particular, $P_{\times}\subseteq X$ satisfies Skula-density condition
\textup{(SD)}.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Write $x=(a,t)$ and let
$C=\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X)}(P^{\times}_{0}\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Xx)$. Clearly $C\subseteq\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Xx$. Fix
$c\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,t)$. Since $\operatorname{supp}(a)$ is finite and the value $c$
occurs infinitely often in $(\theta_i)$, choose
$i\notin\operatorname{supp}(a)$ with $\theta_i=c$. Let $a^{i,n}$ agree with $a$ except
that $a^{i,n}(i)=n$. Then $(a^{i,n})_n$ is increasing with supremum $a$.

For all sufficiently large $n$, one has $\beta_i(n)\leq t$, and hence
\((a^{i,n},\beta_i(n))\in P^{\times}_{0}\cap\mathord{{\downarrow}}_X(a,t)\subseteq C\).
Since $c<\beta_i(n)$ and $C$ is lower, $(a^{i,n},c)\in C$. Taking the
directed supremum over the tail in $n$ gives $(a,c)\in C$. Finally,
\((a,t)=\bigvee\{(a,c):c\in\mathbb Q,\ 0<c<t\}\),
so $x\in C$. Lowerness then gives $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_Xx\subseteq C$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:product-directed-lifting}
The inclusion $P_{\times}\subseteq X$ has directed lifting.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $A\subseteq X$ be directed, write $\bigvee_XA=(a,t)$, and let
$q=(b,r)\in P_{\times}$ satisfy $q\leq(a,t)$. By
\cref{prop:product-P-basic}, $r\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1)$.

Choose $(f_0,s_0)\in A$, put $H=\operatorname{supp}(f_0)$, and let
$A'=A\cap\mathord{\uparrow}_X(f_0,s_0)$. Then $A'$ is directed and cofinal,
$\operatorname{supp}(a)\subseteq H$, and every first coordinate of a point of $A'$ is
$\infty$ outside $H$. Hence $\tau=(a,H,q)\in\mathcal T_{\times}$.

For each $n\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ and $i\in H$, the finite element
$\min\{a(i),n\}$ is compact in $\overline{\mathbb N_{>0}}$ and lies below the
supremum of the $i$th coordinates of $A'$. Together with
$\frac{n}{n+1}r<t$, these finitely many requirements and directedness yield
$y_n=(f_n,s_n)\in A'$ such that
\[
  u^{\times}_{a,H,n}\leq f_n,
  \qquad
  \frac{n}{n+1}r\leq s_n.
\]
Put $q_n=\operatorname{row}_{\times}(\tau,n)$. By \eqref{eq:P-product}, each $q_n$ belongs to
$P_{\times}$, and \cref{lem:product-rows} shows that $(q_n)_n$ is increasing with supremum $q$. Moreover,
\eqref{eq:row-product} yields $q_n\leq y_n$. Thus
$\{q_n:n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\}$ witnesses directed lifting.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:product-Gamma-isomorphism}
The restriction map is an order isomorphism
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product-Gamma-iso}
  \rho:\Gamma(X)\longrightarrow\Gamma(P_{\times}),
  \qquad H\longmapsto H\cap P_{\times}.
\end{equation}
Its inverse is $C\mapsto\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X)}(C)$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
\cref{lem:product-Skula-density} gives \eqref{eq:SD}. By
\cref{prop:product-directed-lifting,prop:directed-lifting-bridge-density},
directed lifting gives \eqref{eq:SC}. Apply \cref{thm:closure-characterization}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:product-sober}
The Scott topology of $X=K\times\mathbb I$ is the product topology of
$\Sigma K$ and $\Sigma\mathbb I$. Consequently, $\Sigma X$ is sober.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Every basic open rectangle $U\times V$, with $U\in\sigma(K)$ and
$V\in\sigma(\mathbb I)$, is Scott open in the product dcpo. Indeed, it is an upper
set. If $E\subseteq K\times\mathbb I$ is directed and
$\bigvee E\in U\times V$, Scott openness of $U$ and $V$ gives
$e_1,e_2\in E$ whose first and second coordinates lie in $U$ and $V$,
respectively. Directedness yields $e\in E$ with $e_1,e_2\leq e$, and then
$e\in U\times V$. Hence the product topology is contained in $\sigma(X)$.

For the reverse inclusion, let $W\in\sigma(X)$ and $(a,t)\in W$. Since
\((a,t)=\bigvee\{(a,s):0<s<t\}\),
Scott openness gives $0<s<t$ with $(a,s)\in W$. For this fixed $s$, the map
\(\iota_s:K\longrightarrow K\times\mathbb I,\qquad b\longmapsto(b,s)\),
preserves directed suprema and is therefore Scott continuous. Consequently
its inverse image
\(W_s=\iota_s^{-1}(W)=\{b\in K:(b,s)\in W\}\)
is Scott open in $K$. The interval $(s,1]$ is Scott open in the chain
$\mathbb I$. Since $W$ is an upper set,
\((a,t)\in W_s\times(s,1]\subseteq W\).
Thus every Scott-open neighbourhood contains a product-open neighbourhood,
and the two topologies agree. Both $\Sigma K$ and $\Sigma\mathbb I$ are sober: the former by \cref{prop:K-sober}, the latter because $\mathbb I$ is continuous. Topological products of sober spaces are sober \cite{goubault2013}, so $\Sigma X$ is sober.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:product-counterexample}
There exists a countable sober $C_{\sigma}$-unique dcpo $K$ such that,
for the continuous chain $\mathbb I=(0,1]$, the product $K\times\mathbb I$ is sober but
not $C_{\sigma}$-unique. More precisely, $K\times\mathbb I$ has a proper
countable $2$-equable sub-dcpo $P_{\times}$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product-counterexample}
  \Gamma(K\times\mathbb I)\cong\Gamma(P_{\times}),
  \qquad
  K\times\mathbb I\not\cong P_{\times}.
\end{equation}
Thus the class of $C_{\sigma}$-unique dcpos is not closed under binary
products.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The dcpo $K$ is countable, sober and $C_{\sigma}$-unique by
\cref{prop:product-factor-order,prop:K-sober,thm:K-unique}, while
$\mathbb I$ is continuous and $C_{\sigma}$-unique. The product is sober by \cref{prop:product-sober}. By
\cref{prop:product-P-basic,thm:product-P-dcpo,thm:product-Gamma-isomorphism},
$P_{\times}$ is a proper countable $2$-equable sub-dcpo of
$X=K\times\mathbb I$ and has no greatest element. Since $X$ has greatest
element $(\top_K,1)$, one has $P_{\times}\not\cong X$, so
\eqref{eq:product-counterexample} shows that $X$ is not
$C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:coordinate-frame}
The poset $\mathcal A$ is a countable algebraic frame. Arbitrary joins and meets are
set-theoretic unions and intersections.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Lower sets are closed under arbitrary unions and intersections, and
intersection distributes over arbitrary union. Hence $\mathcal A$ is a frame.

Let $U$ be an upper set of a wqo. Its minimal elements form an antichain and
are therefore finite. Every $u\in U$ lies above a minimal member of $U$:
otherwise one can recursively choose
$u=u_0>u_1>u_2>\cdots$ inside $U$, contradicting well-foundedness. Hence
$U$ is generated by its finite set of minimal elements. It follows that every
lower set has the form $\mathfrak R\setminus\mathord{\uparrow} F$ for some finite
$F\subseteq\mathfrak R$. Since $\mathfrak R$ is countable, only countably many such $F$
occur, and $\mathcal A$ is countable.

Every lower set $U$ is the directed union of $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\mathfrak R}F$, where $F$
ranges over the finite subsets of $U$. Such a finitely generated lower set
is compact: if $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\mathfrak R}F$ is contained in a directed union of lower
sets, finitely many members cover $F$, and one common upper member of the
directed family contains all of $\mathord{{\downarrow}}_{\mathfrak R}F$. Hence $\mathcal A$ is algebraic.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:markers}
The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em]
\item Each $t_n$ is finite and lower,
      $t_0\subsetneq t_1\subsetneq\cdots$, and
      $\bigcup_nt_n=\top_{\mathcal A}$.
\item
      \(
        D_m=\{(i,j)\in\mathfrak R:j<m\}\cup\{(m,j):m<j\}.
      \)
\item $t_n\subseteq e_n\subsetneq\top_{\mathcal A}$ for every $n$.
\item $(e_n)_{n<\omega}$ is an antichain in $\mathcal A$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The assertions about $t_n$ are immediate from \eqref{eq:rado}. An element
$(i,j)$ lies below some $(m,\ell)$ with $m<\ell$ exactly when $j<m$ or
$i=m$, proving the formula for $D_m$. If $(i,j)\in t_n$, then
$j\leq n+1<n+2$, so $(i,j)\in D_{n+2}=e_n$. Moreover, $e_n\subsetneq\top_{\mathcal A}$, since $(n+3,n+4)\notin e_n$.

For $a<b$,
\[
  (a,b)\in D_a\setminus D_b,
  \qquad
  (b,b+1)\in D_b\setminus D_a.
\]
Thus the $D_m$, and hence the shifted family $(e_n)$, are pairwise
incomparable.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:F-frame}
The poset $F$ is a countable frame. For every nonempty family
$\mathcal B\subseteq F_0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:profile-join}
  \left(\bigvee\mathcal B\right)(s)
  =\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal B}f(s).
\end{equation}
If $\mathcal B\subseteq F_0$ and
$U=\bigcup_{f\in\mathcal B}\operatorname{supp}(f)$ is finite, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:profile-meet}
  \left(\bigwedge\mathcal B\right)(s)
  =\bigcap_{f\in\mathcal B}f(s),
\end{equation}
where the empty intersection is $\top_{\mathcal A}$; if $U$ is infinite, then
$\bigwedge\mathcal B=\bot_F$. The join of the empty family is $\bot_F$,
bottom terms may be discarded from a nonempty join, and any meet containing
$\bot_F$ is $\bot_F$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Countability follows because $S$ and $\mathcal A$ are countable and every profile
has finite support. For \eqref{eq:profile-join}, fix
$f_0\in\mathcal B$. Outside $\operatorname{supp}(f_0)$ the coordinate union is $\top_{\mathcal A}$, so
it again has finite support and is plainly the least upper bound. If $U$ is
finite, the coordinate intersection in \eqref{eq:profile-meet} is the greatest
lower bound in $F_0$. If $U$ is infinite, a nonbottom common lower bound would
have non-top value at every coordinate of $U$, contradicting finite support;
thus the meet is $\bot_F$.

It remains to verify the frame law. The empty family and the case in which
all $g_i$ are bottom are immediate. Otherwise discard the bottom terms.
Finite meets are then coordinatewise intersections, and for $f\in F_0$,
\[
  \left(f\wedge\bigvee_i g_i\right)(s)
  =f(s)\cap\bigcup_i g_i(s)
  =\bigcup_i(f(s)\cap g_i(s))
  =\left(\bigvee_i(f\wedge g_i)\right)(s).
\]
The case $f=\bot_F$ and the empty family are immediate.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:profile-not-algebraic}
Although $\mathcal A$ is algebraic, $F$ is not. For a nonbottom profile $f$, choose $r\notin\operatorname{supp}(f)$ and let $f_n$ agree with $f$ except that $f_n(r)=t_n$. Then $(f_n)_n$ is increasing, every $f_n<f$, and $\bigvee_n f_n=f$. Hence no nonbottom element of $F$ is compact.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:canonical-approximants}
The sequence $(u^{F}_{\tau,n})$ is increasing and has supremum $a$. Moreover,
if $(y_k)$ is an increasing sequence of nonbottom profiles with supremum
$a$, then its supports are eventually a fixed finite set $H$, and for every
$n$ some $k$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:u-below}
  u^{F}_{(a,H),n}\leq y_k.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The first assertion follows coordinatewise from $\bigcup_nt_n=\top_{\mathcal A}$. Supports decrease along an increasing sequence and hence eventually stabilize at a finite set $H$. One has $\operatorname{supp}(a)\subseteq H$, but equality is not required: a coordinate may reach $\top_{\mathcal A}$ only at the supremum. At each coordinate,
$a(s)=\bigcup_ky_k(s)$. For fixed $n$ and $s\in H$, the set
$u^{F}_{(a,H),n}(s)$ is finite and contained in $a(s)$, so it is contained in
some sufficiently late $y_k(s)$. One common $k$ works for all coordinates
in finite $H$; outside $H$ both profiles have value $\top_{\mathcal A}$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:rows}
For every eligible pair $(\tau,q)$, the rows increase to $q$:
\[
  \bigvee_n\operatorname{row}_{F}(\tau,q,n)=q.
\]
At the private coordinate $k=h_F(\tau,q)$,
$\operatorname{row}_{F}(\tau,q,n)(k)=t_n$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Put $k=h_F(\tau,q)$. The meet in \eqref{eq:row} is coordinatewise intersection. At $k$, both $q$ and $u^{F}_{\tau,n}$ have value $\top_{\mathcal A}$, so the row has value $t_n$. At every other coordinate,
\[
  \bigcup_n\operatorname{row}_{F}(\tau,q,n)(s)
  =q(s)\cap\bigcup_nu^{F}_{\tau,n}(s)
  =q(s)\cap a(s)=q(s),
\]
using $q\leq a$. At the private coordinate the union of the $t_n$ is
$\top_{\mathcal A}=q(k)$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:P-dcpo}
The inherited order makes $P_F$ a dcpo, and all directed suprema in $P_F$ agree
with those in $F$. Thus $P_F\subseteq F$ is a sub-dcpo.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Give every nonbottom retained profile a certificate. If it has a coordinate
with value $e_i$, choose one such coordinate and call it a marker
certificate. Otherwise choose a row representation
$p=\operatorname{row}_{F}(\tau,q,n)$ from the least stage at which $p$ appears and use its
private coordinate as a row certificate. At that coordinate the value is
$t_n$. Injectivity of $h_F$ means that a row-certificate coordinate determines
$(\tau,q)$, while the value $t_n$ determines the row level $n$ because the
sequence $(t_n)$ is strictly increasing.  Thus, after a certificate type and
coordinate have been fixed, the corresponding subsequence is controlled by a
single marker family or a single private row family.

Let $p_0\leq p_1\leq\cdots$ be increasing in $P_F$. If every term equals $\bot_F$, the conclusion is immediate. Otherwise discard the finitely many terms before the first nonbottom term and reindex. Let $p=\bigvee_F p_k$. Supports decrease, so
$\operatorname{supp}(p_k)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$ for all $k$, and therefore
$\operatorname{supp}(p)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$; in particular $p\in F_0$. Every certificate
coordinate also belongs to the finite set $\operatorname{supp}(p_0)$. There are only two
certificate types and only finitely many possible certificate coordinates.
Hence one certificate type and one coordinate occur on an infinite
subsequence. Its set of indices is unbounded, so the subsequence is cofinal
in the original sequence and has the same ambient supremum $p$.

In the marker case, at a fixed coordinate $s$ we have
$p_{k_j}(s)=e_{i_j}$. Comparability gives
$e_{i_j}\subseteq e_{i_{j+1}}$, and the antichain property forces all
$i_j$ to equal one $i$. For $k_j\leq k\leq k_{j+1}$,
\(e_i=p_{k_j}(s)\subseteq p_k(s)\subseteq p_{k_{j+1}}(s)=e_i\).
Thus the original sequence is eventually $e_i$ at $s$. Consequently the
ambient supremum $p$ satisfies $p(s)=e_i$; since $p\in F_0$, it follows from
\eqref{eq:P0} that $p\in P^{F}_{0}$.

In the row case, the fixed private coordinate determines one pair
$(\tau,q)$, so the cofinal subsequence is $\operatorname{row}_{F}(\tau,q,n_j)$. At the private
coordinate its values are $t_{n_j}$; comparability makes $(n_j)$
nondecreasing. If it is bounded, it is eventually constant, so the cofinal
subsequence, and hence the original sequence, has a retained row as its
supremum. If it is unbounded, it is cofinal in the full row sequence and has
supremum $q$ by \cref{lem:rows}; this $q$ lies in an earlier construction
stage. Hence every increasing sequence has its $F$-supremum in $P_F$.

Since $P_F$ is countable, every directed subset has an increasing cofinal
sequence. Its supremum therefore belongs to $P_F$ and is the same in $P_F$ and
$F$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:frame-approximation-properties}
The inclusion $P_F\subseteq F$ has directed lifting and bridge density.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
For directed lifting, let $E\subseteq F$ be directed, put $a=\bigvee E$, and
let $q\in P_F$ satisfy $q\leq a$. If $q=\bot_F$, use $\{\bot_F\}$. Otherwise,
$F$ is countable by \cref{thm:F-frame}, so choose an increasing cofinal
sequence $(y_k)$ in $E$ and delete its initial bottom terms. The supports
stabilize at a finite set $H$, necessarily containing $\operatorname{supp}(a)$. By
\cref{lem:canonical-approximants}, for each $n$ there is $k(n)$ with
$u^{F}_{(a,H),n}\leq y_{k(n)}$. Since $q\leq a$, the pair $((a,H),q)$ is eligible.
Let $b_n=\operatorname{row}_{F}((a,H),q,n)$. If $q\in P^{F}_{m}$, then $b_n\in P^{F}_{m+1}$ by
\eqref{eq:Pm}; moreover, $b_n\leq y_{k(n)}$ and $\bigvee_n b_n=q$ by
\cref{lem:rows}. Thus $(b_n)$ witnesses directed lifting.

For bridge density, the bottom element is immediate. Given $a\in F_0$, choose
$r\notin\operatorname{supp}(a)$ and define
\[
  v_n(s)=
  \begin{cases}
    t_n,&s=r,\\
    a(s),&s\neq r,
  \end{cases}
  \qquad
  c_n(s)=
  \begin{cases}
    e_n,&s=r,\\
    a(s),&s\neq r.
  \end{cases}
\]
Then $v_n\leq c_n\leq a$, the point $c_n$ belongs to $P^{F}_{0}$, and
$\bigvee_n v_n=a$. Hence $(v_n,c_n)$ witnesses bridge density. This is the
only place where the inclusions $t_n\subseteq e_n$ are used.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:Gamma-isomorphism}
The restriction map is an order isomorphism
\[
  \rho:\Gamma(F)\longrightarrow\Gamma(P_F),
  \qquad \rho(C)=C\cap P_F.
\]
Its inverse is $C\mapsto\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(F)}(C)$.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Apply \cref{prop:directed-lifting-bridge-density} to
\cref{thm:P-dcpo,prop:frame-approximation-properties}.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:P-not-isomorphic-F}
The dcpo $P_F$ has no greatest element. Therefore $P_F\not\cong F$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
First, $\top_F\notin P_F$: it has no marker coordinate, so it is not in $P^{F}_{0}$,
and every nonbottom row has value $t_n\neq\top_{\mathcal A}$ at its private coordinate.
This persists through all stages $P^{F}_{m}$.

If $p=\bot_F$, any nonbottom marker profile is not below $p$. Let
$p\neq\bot_F$. Since $p\neq\top_F$, its support is nonempty and finite. Choose
$r\notin\operatorname{supp}(p)$ and let $m_r$ have value $e_0$ at $r$ and $\top_{\mathcal A}$
elsewhere. Then $m_r\in P^{F}_{0}$, but for any $s\in\operatorname{supp}(p)$ one has
$m_r(s)=\top_{\mathcal A}\not\subseteq p(s)$, so $m_r\not\leq p$. Thus $P_F$ has no
greatest element, whereas $F$ has greatest element $\top_F$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:countable-frame-counterexample}
There exist a countable frame $F$ and a countable dcpo $P_F$ such that
\[
  \Gamma(F)\cong\Gamma(P_F),
  \qquad F\not\cong P_F.
\]
Moreover, $\Sigma F$ is sober. Hence a sober countable frame need not be
$C_{\sigma}$-unique.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
The poset $F$ is a countable frame by \cref{thm:F-frame}, and $P_F$ is a
countable dcpo by \cref{thm:P-dcpo}. The isomorphism of Scott-closed-set
lattices is \cref{thm:Gamma-isomorphism}, while
\cref{prop:P-not-isomorphic-F} gives $F\not\cong P_F$. Finally, every
countable frame is Scott sober \cite[Theorem~1.1]{XuJi2026}.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
\label{q:locally-compact-sober}
Is every locally compact sober dcpo $C_{\sigma}$-unique?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{q:product-stability}
What structural conditions on a family \((D_i)_{i\in I}\) of
\(C_{\sigma}\)-unique dcpos guarantee that
\(
  \prod_{i\in I}D_i
\)
is again \(C_{\sigma}\)-unique?
<!-- end question-2 -->
